balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Transurban Group: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Transurban Group: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Transurban Group: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Transurban Group: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Transurban Group: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Transurban Group: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Transurban Group: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Transurban Group: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Transurban Group: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

trafficByCity.title: Average daily traffic by city
trafficByCity.content:
Average daily traffic is the average number of vehicle trips per day across each city network over the financial year, in thousands.

For Transurban Group: traffic is the physical volume driver behind toll revenue -- growth here is actual usage, not just price. Sydney (WestConnex, M5, M2, M7, Lane Cove) and Melbourne (CityLink) are the two largest networks; the Greater Washington/Virginia express lanes (North America) are the newest and fastest-growing.

What to watch:

  • Traffic growth versus toll revenue growth -- a gap is toll escalation (CPI-linked or fixed-rate) doing the work
  • Any city lagging the others (COVID-style commuting shifts, new free alternative routes)
  • Only disclosed at full-year, so half-year rows are blank

tollRevenueByCity.title: Toll revenue by city
tollRevenueByCity.content:
Toll revenue by city asset, plus Transurban's own proportional toll revenue (its pro-rata share across all toll roads, including equity-accounted joint ventures the four city columns don't cover on a 100% basis).

For Transurban Group: Sydney is now the largest contributor following the WestConnex ramp-up; North America is the smallest but has the highest growth rate as the Virginia express lanes mature.

What to watch:

  • Which city is driving group growth in a given year
  • The gap between the sum of the four cities and the proportional total -- that gap is minority-owned JV toll roads outside the four core networks
  • Toll escalation mechanisms differ by road (CPI vs fixed % vs uncapped) and by Australian state regulation

proportionalFreeCash.title: Proportional EBITDA and free cash
proportionalFreeCash.content:
Proportional operating EBITDA is Transurban's pro-rata share of EBITDA across every toll road it holds, including minority-owned joint ventures consolidated at less than 100% -- the measure management actually targets, distinct from the statutory group EBITDA charted above. Free cash is Transurban's own distribution-funding cash measure (distributions have historically been set with reference to it, not statutory free cash flow); free cash ex capital releases strips out one-off proceeds from asset recycling (selling down stakes) or refinancing.

For Transurban Group: as a toll-road operator carrying ~A$27bn of debt against long-dated concession assets, the distribution is the reason most holders own the stock -- free cash sets the ceiling on it.

What to watch:

  • Free cash running below the ex-capital-releases line for consecutive years (distributions outrunning sustainable cash generation)
  • Proportional EBITDA growth versus statutory EBITDA growth -- a widening gap means the JV portfolio mix is shifting

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Transurban Group: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
